title: How to Use the Resend API Without Hitting Rate Limits
summary: Resend API documentation covers authentication, rate limits, and pricing. Evaluate service fit, budget costs, troubleshoot errors, and optimize requests.
body_markdown:
## Resend API rate limit 429s at launch


You can sit well inside a daily quota and still run into a limit that resets every second, and at launch the second is the one that bites.


In a modelled scenario (not a vendor figure), 1,000 sign-up emails arrive in one minute. At the default 10 requests per second, documented on[Resend's rate-limit page](https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/rate-limit) , only 600 of them are accepted, so you cannot exceed this throughput.


**400 of them come back as 429s** . That's 40 percent of the people who just signed up, staring at a screen waiting for a code that was never sent.


Read the 400 as users, not requests, which means each is a real person. Each one is someone who typed an address, pressed the button and got nothing.


Chart: Where 1,000 launch-minute sign-up emails end up


**Unless your code retries, those 400 are lost.** The API doesn't queue them for you, and nothing in your dashboard will look broken, because the 600 that went through look healthy.


### What a Resend 429 response contains


When a request is rejected, it returns HTTP status 429, which means too many requests. In this scenario that status arrives 400 times in one minute, so your error handling isn't an edge case; it carries 40 percent of your traffic.


Per the same rate-limit page, the response carries headers that report your limit and how much of it remains. Another header tells you how long to wait before trying again.


Log those headers. They tell you how far over the limit you were and how long to back off, which is the difference between a retry that works and one that adds to the pile.


If you retry immediately and without delay, you spend the next second's allowance on the same emails and push newer sign-ups into the rejected group.


Not everyone sending these emails is a developer, and the low-volume case doesn't need any of the retry code above.


Describe the notification to the built-in chat in Activepieces, say a form submission that emails the new user through Resend, and it builds and publishes the flow in your account, with a run trace you can open for every execution to see what happened.


It runs under the same RBAC and audit logs as a flow built by hand, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production. It doesn't replace the API for the launch-minute burst above, which stays in code where you control the backoff.


### Daily quota versus per-second limit


Treat them as two limits, because they measure different things. A quota counts total sends over a day or a month; the per-second limit counts how many requests arrive in the same moment.


The scenario above could sit well inside any quota and still lose 400 emails.


1,000 requests in 60 seconds is an average of about 17 per second, and real bursts are rarely even.


A monthly allowance only tells you how much you may send. The per-second limit tells you how quickly you may ask, so check both before launch.
